o: Calculate raw mono sound storage in bits and bytes.
Calculate text storage when the encoding size is specified.
Show clear workings and units without a calculator.
r: Explain the difference between sound sample rate and bit depth.
Sample rate is samples taken per second; bit depth is bits used to store each sample.
Why is Unicode useful for multilingual text?
It represents many more characters and writing systems than standard ASCII.
Convert 4,000 bits into bytes.
Mono sound is sampled at 1,000 Hz, four bits per sample, for two seconds. Calculate the raw data size in bits and bytes.
c: Raw mono sound
sample rate × duration × bit depth gives bits, assuming one channel and no compression.
Convert units
Divide by 8 for bytes. At this level use the conversion stated in the exam question for KB and MB.
Text files
If each character is stored in one byte, n characters take approximately n bytes before metadata/compression.
Check your assumptions
Unicode can use varying numbers of bytes per character. Never assume all text uses one byte unless stated.
Exam technique
Write the formula and units, even if the final calculation is simple.

m.q: Find the uncompressed size of 3 seconds of mono sound at 1,000 samples/s and 8 bits/sample.
st: Sample rate = 1,000 per second. Duration = 3 seconds. Bit depth = 8.
State assumption: raw mono data only, no header or compression.

w: Find raw bits for 2 s of mono sound at 2,000 Hz and 4-bit depth.
Convert 16,000 bits to bytes.
2,000 bytes.
A message contains 250 characters at 8 bits each. What size in bytes?

k.q: Create a sound-file size calculation on your mini-whiteboard.
k.code:
rate = 1000
seconds = 3
depth = 8
print(rate * seconds * depth)
p: Change seconds to 5 and predict again.
Write a print instruction to display the size in bytes.
k.a: 24,000 bits initially; 40,000 bits with 5 seconds; print(rate * seconds * depth DIV 8) displays 5,000 bytes for 5 s.

e: Calculate bits needed for 4 s of 500 Hz mono sound using 8 bits per sample. [3]
Convert 16,000 bits to bytes. [2]
A text file contains 600 characters stored using eight bits each. Give its size in bytes, ignoring metadata. [2]
v: One measurement or cycle per second; used for sample rate.
Number of bits used per sound sample.
Method of representing characters or samples with binary.
x: A mono sound file’s raw bit count increases when the recording gets longer.

o: Select suitable compression for a given scenario.
r: Calculate the raw bit size of three seconds of mono sound sampled at 2,000 Hz with eight-bit depth.
What does bitmap colour depth measure?
The number of bits used for each pixel.
What is a character set?
A mapping between characters and numerical/binary codes.
A file contains 15 characters at eight bits each and a 4 × 4 bitmap at two bits per pixel. Calculate the combined raw data size in bytes, ignoring metadata.
Text = 120 bits; image = 32 bits; total = 152 bits = 19 bytes.
c: Compression
Reduces file size, helping storage and transmission.
Lossless
Original data can be perfectly reconstructed; important for code, documents and other files that must remain exact.
Lossy
Discards some information judged less noticeable. May achieve smaller files but original is not perfectly restored.
Choices depend on context
Text files need exact recovery; online photography can sometimes tolerate quality loss; medical or scientific images may not.
Not examined at algorithm level
OCR J277 expects the principle and scenarios; designing run-length/Huffman compression is not required.

m.q: Choose how to compress a school website’s text files and promotional photographs.
st: For HTML or program files, no character or instruction may be lost.
Choose lossless compression so original text/code can be fully recovered.
For a large photographic banner, some quality reduction may be acceptable.
Choose lossy compression if a smaller download is more valuable than perfect pixel recovery.
Justify using the actual needs of each file, not simply which is 'better'.

w: Why must a Python source file use lossless compression?
A missing or altered character could break code; it must be restored exactly.
Choose for a social-media photo where small file size matters.
Lossy can be appropriate; accept reduced quality in exchange for smaller size.
What could make lossless better than lossy for an archival original?
Preserving every bit ensures the file can be recovered exactly for future use.

k.q: Model a change in file size using simple code.
p: Predict how many storage units were saved.
Change compressed to 450 and predict the saving.
Write a second print instruction that shows the remaining compressed size.
k.a: 300 units saved initially; 450 saved after change; print(compressed) displays 450. This models the result, not a compression algorithm.

e: Give one reason for compressing a file before emailing it. [1]
Reduces file size so it transmits faster or uses less bandwidth/storage.
A program’s source code must be stored exactly. Select a compression type and justify. [3]
Lossless: decompression recreates every bit exactly; a change to program instructions could prevent it from working.
Explain why lossy compression may be suitable for a video clip. [2]
Some data can be removed to reduce file size; slight quality loss may be acceptable to the viewer.
v: Reducing the number of bits needed to store a file.
Compression from which the exact original can be recovered.
Compression that removes some information permanently.
Reconstructing or extracting data from a compressed file.
x: Lossy compression can always restore every original bit.

011.t: Primary Storage: RAM, ROM and Cache
o: Explain why primary storage is necessary.
Compare RAM and ROM and explain cache.
Apply memory concepts to a real computer.
r: What is the difference between lossy and lossless compression?
Lossless allows exact reconstruction; lossy permanently discards some information.
What is the difference between sound sample rate and bit depth?
Sample rate is samples per second; bit depth is bits per sample.
Perform a two-place logical right shift on 00110100.
A school needs to compress a program's source code and a photograph for its website. Recommend an appropriate compression method for each and justify your choices.
Source code: lossless, to preserve every character. Photograph: lossy may be acceptable to reduce size if some visual quality loss is tolerable.
c: Why a computer needs primary storage
The processor needs quick access to data and instructions being used now.
RAM
Main working memory: read/write and volatile. Data usually disappears when power is removed.
ROM
Non-volatile storage containing fixed/firmware startup instructions; retains contents without power.
Cache
Very fast memory near/in the CPU for frequently accessed data and instructions; reduces slower RAM accesses.
Memory versus storage
RAM is working memory; SSD/HDD are long-term secondary storage. Cache, RAM and ROM have different jobs.

m.q: A laptop starts up, opens a game, and then shuts down. Identify where information is stored.
st: On start-up, ROM/firmware contains instructions to begin loading the system.
The operating system and game are loaded from secondary storage into RAM.
The CPU reads needed data and instructions from RAM; frequently used items can be cached.
As the game runs, RAM changes; cache speeds repeated access.
On power-off, RAM loses its data. Saved game files remain on secondary storage.

w: A word processor is running. Which memory stores its working data?
RAM.
Which type retains start-up firmware after power is removed?
ROM or other non-volatile firmware storage.
Why does the CPU use cache despite having RAM?
Cache is faster and holds frequently accessed information, reducing RAM access latency.

k.q: Model the difference between a saved value and a changing working value.
p: Explain why an assigned variable models changing data in RAM, not real physical ROM.
k.a: Displays 10 then 15. With the change, 10 then 20. An OCR ERL variable is a classroom model of working data; it does not simulate memory hardware.

e: State one difference between RAM and ROM. [2]
RAM is volatile/read-write working memory; ROM is non-volatile and normally holds firmware.
Explain why a CPU uses cache memory. [2]
Frequently needed data/instructions can be accessed faster than from RAM, improving average performance.
An embedded device must start correctly after losing power. Explain which memory may hold its start-up instructions. [2]
ROM/non-volatile firmware retains start-up instructions when power is off.
v: Volatile working memory for active programs/data.
Small, very fast memory used to speed repeated CPU access.
Loses stored data when power is removed.
x: RAM normally retains the data of running programs after power is removed.

o: Explain why virtual memory may be needed.
Describe moving data between RAM and secondary storage.
Explain the performance cost of excessive swapping.
r: Explain one difference between RAM and ROM.
RAM is volatile working memory. ROM is non-volatile and commonly stores firmware.
A 300 × 100 bitmap uses four bits per pixel. Calculate its raw pixel-data size in bytes.
Why is lossless compression suitable for program files?
The exact original instructions must be recovered; lost or changed characters could break the program.
Explain why the CPU benefits from cache memory but cannot use a small cache as a complete replacement for main RAM.
Cache is very fast but small; it holds frequently needed data/instructions. RAM has much greater capacity for active programs and data.
c: When RAM is insufficient
The operating system can use part of secondary storage as virtual memory.
Data moves between locations
Inactive pages of a program can be stored on secondary storage so RAM can hold data needed now.
Virtual memory is slower
SSDs/HDDs have much slower access than RAM, so swapping can slow a computer.
A common misunderstanding
Virtual memory is not extra physical RAM. It allows the system to use secondary storage when needed.
Context
Too many open applications can cause heavy swapping and poor responsiveness.

m.q: A computer has 4 GB RAM but the active programs need 6 GB. What happens?
st: Compare required memory 6 GB with available RAM 4 GB.
The deficit is 6 − 4 = 2 GB.
Operating system moves some less-needed memory pages to secondary storage.
When those pages are required, the system transfers data back, possibly moving other pages out.
Repeated transfers slow performance because secondary storage is slower than RAM.

w: Where is virtual memory stored?
In part of secondary storage such as an SSD or HDD.
Why does heavy swapping slow a computer?
Data is being transferred between RAM and slower secondary storage.
Does virtual memory increase the amount of installed RAM?
No. It uses secondary storage as an extension of available memory.

k.q: Model a memory shortfall with arithmetic.
p: Predict the required extra capacity in GB.
Write a line to print zero when sufficient RAM is available (no IF needed: choose a suitable value).
k.a: 2 GB shortfall initially; 1 GB when ram = 5; choose required = 4, ram = 4 and the subtraction prints 0. This is a simple capacity model, not a simulation of virtual memory.

e: Define virtual memory. [2]
Part of secondary storage temporarily used to hold data/instructions when RAM is insufficient.
Describe the movement of data when RAM becomes full. [3]
Less-used data/pages move from RAM to secondary storage; required pages return to RAM when needed; this frees RAM for active processes.
Explain a possible effect of virtual memory on performance. [2]
Slower disk/SSD access and frequent swapping can delay program execution compared with RAM.
v: Secondary storage used as an extension when RAM is insufficient.
A unit of memory data moved between RAM and backing storage.
Transfer memory data between RAM and secondary storage.
Non-volatile storage such as an SSD or HDD.
x: Virtual memory usually operates at the same speed as physical RAM.

o: Explain why secondary storage is needed.
Compare magnetic, optical and solid-state technologies.
r: Why can using virtual memory make a computer slower?
Data must be moved between RAM and slower secondary storage; frequent swapping causes delays.
State one difference between RAM and ROM.
RAM is volatile/read-write working memory; ROM is non-volatile firmware storage.
State one advantage of Unicode over ASCII.
It can represent many more characters from different scripts.
A computer has 4 GB of RAM, but its active applications require 7 GB. Explain how the computer may continue running and why performance could decrease.
There is a 3 GB shortfall. The OS may use secondary storage as virtual memory, moving pages between RAM and storage; this is slower than accessing RAM.
c: Why secondary storage exists
It preserves programs, files and data after power is removed.
Magnetic
Hard disk drives offer large capacity at relatively low price per GB; moving parts make them vulnerable to knocks.
Optical
CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs use lasers; portable/removable, often slower and lower capacity than SSDs/HDDs.
Solid state
SSDs and flash drives have no moving parts, fast access and good portability, typically at a higher price per GB than HDDs.
Compare in context
OCR asks about capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost.

m.q: A film-editing workstation needs fast storage for active files and cheap capacity for archives.
st: Identify need one: fast access to current large video files.
Recommend SSD for working projects: high access speed and no moving parts.
Identify need two: lots of long-term storage on a budget.
Recommend HDD for archives: often lower cost per GB for large capacities.
Explain that either must be backed up; the storage type does not guarantee data safety.

w: Name one magnetic storage device.
Hard disk drive (HDD).
Name one optical storage medium.
DVD, CD or Blu-ray.
Why is an SSD often suitable for a laptop?
Fast, durable against knocks, and no moving parts.

k.q: Calculate how many files fit into a drive.
p: Predict how many equal-sized files fit.
Explain why storage capacity alone does not tell us which drive is best.
k.a: 5 files initially; 4 files when fileSize = 250. Speed, durability, reliability, portability and cost also matter. Units must match.

e: Name three technologies used for secondary storage. [3]
Magnetic, optical, solid state.
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of an SSD compared with an HDD. [4]
Advantage: faster access / more resistant to shocks because no moving parts. Disadvantage: commonly higher purchase cost per GB.
Justify a suitable storage device for a school’s high-capacity, low-cost backup. [3]
HDD: large capacity and lower cost per GB; suitable for backups where maximum speed is less important.
v: Stores bits through magnetic properties, e.g. HDD.
Uses a laser to access disc data, e.g. DVD.
Stores bits electronically with no moving parts, e.g. SSD.
x: An HDD generally has no moving mechanical parts.
